title: K-2 students no longer get personal iPads, Seattle superintendent says, pledging less screen time
text:
Seattle Public Schools is tightening screen time and device access for its youngest students.

Speaking from the district office on Monday afternoon, Superintendent Ben Shuldiner announced SPS will no longer send iPads home with students in kindergarten through second grade. Additionally, screen time in the classroom for those students will be capped at 30 minutes per day.

“There's no reason why a kindergarten kid needs to have an iPad every day in their hand,” Shuldiner said. “That just doesn't make any sense to me.  People learned way before iPads were invented.”

The reversal marks a turnaround from pandemic-era learning, when schools and families scrambled to get computers in the hands of students, so they could log online to learn. But kids have been back in schools for in-person learning for several years, and the one-device-per-student policy represents a vestige of the pandemic that’s still “hanging around,” according to Shuldiner.

Shuldiner laid out a model where classrooms have their own set of tablets that teachers can “wheel in” and use whenever the curriculum calls for it.

There may still be moments when learning happens on screens, however. The district’s newly adopted English language arts curriculum does include a block of screen time for small group learning, and that’s one of the reasons why the district isn’t banning screens entirely. But moving forward, Shuldiner said, there needs to be a “high bar” for using technology with young students.

“We can't use iPads or laptops as a kind of, ‘Oh, here's some games to play while we're doing other work,’” Shuldiner said. “We want to make sure that if we are going to use technology, we are intentional about it and rather than using it to watch cartoons or things like that.”

Parents received an email about the new rules on Monday afternoon.

Mike Starosky, the assistant superintendent for academics, said the transition may take longer for some schools, but the district aims to see the rules implemented for students in kindergarten through second grade across the district by Jan. 1.

With roughly 50,000 students in the district, Shuldiner said he wants to assess the changes over the next few months before they possibly expand the policies to older elementary students.The superintendent added he would “love to see” something rolled out for secondary students by the second semester.

Charlotte Taylor, a spokesperson for the advocacy group Seattle Families for Intentional Tech, said she believes the new rules will have a “really positive impact” on the district’s youngest learners, but there’s more work to be done. Taylor said the group also would like to extend the screen time cap to all grades, and see a pause on generative AI for students.

“There’s a lot of great studies out there that show advantages of pencil-and-pen learning over digital apps learning at certain times,” Taylor said. “We really need to be cutting edge as a district, reacting to the research, reacting to other best practices.”

Hilary Patterson, a former Cleveland High School math teacher, also spoke on behalf of the advocacy group. Returning to the classroom after the pandemic, Patterson said she used online learning tools she’d utilized during remote learning because they helped some kids learn. But then, she started to ruminate on a bigger question.

“Is their learning better than if we were doing it a different way?” Patterson said.

In her experience, there’s little or no collaboration when students are tied to their screens, and they’re less likely to engage with a teacher, too. Patterson decided to switch up her own teaching methods.

Instead of having students watch a video on a subject on their individual screens, Patterson said she projected the video onto a single screen for everyone to view. Then, everyone could turn to their classmates, and talk about what they had just learned.
